newsitem.title: FINLAND: Yeltsin's wife set to fade into summit background.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's wife set to fade into summit background.

text.p: Russian first lady Naina Yeltsin, a far cry from the glamorous Raisa Gorbachev, is likely to stay firmly in the background when her husband and U.S. President Bill Clinton meet this week.
Naina -- a wallflower with a steady, motherly image -- turns the clock back to the Soviet era when Kremlin wives were rarely seen or heard and she turns her back on publicity.
"I am only the president's wife. I shudder when people call me the first lady," she has been quoted as saying.
Her image is a stark contrast to the attractive and well-dressed Gorbachev, who impressed in the West but attracted criticism at home for being outspoken.
Naina, who turned 65 last week, will not be joined in Helsinki by Clinton's wife Hillary, who is on a six-nation goodwill tour of Africa with her daughter Chelsea.

It has been reported that Naina is travelling mainly to keep an eye on her husband's health. Yeltsin underwent heart bypass surgery in November and then developed pneumonia, although he has bounced back to health.
Naina's programme will be low-key in Finland.

Finnish president Martti Ahtisaari's wife Eeva will accompany Naina on Friday to a senior citizens' activity centre and a nursery in central Helsinki and the former home of nineteenth century Finnish artist Akseli Gallen-Kallela.
In the afternoon, Naina will visit Finland's National Opera to see a rehersal of Don Quixote.
On Saturday Naina and Eeva will visit a science centre before joining their husbands and President Clinton for a lunch at the presidental palace.

Popular at home for her down-to-earth image, well-wishers sent Naina over a million roses for her 65th bithday last week, according to the Russian news agency Itar-Tass, which appeared to be employing a little poetic license.
Both she and Boris graduated in 1956 with construction engineering degrees from the polytechnical institute in Sverdlovsk, Boris's birthplace.
In 1988, she gave up her job in Sverdlovsk and joined her husband, then first secretary of the Moscow city party committee.
Naina has said that her main duty is to be a good wife, mother and grandmother and that she has no desire to enter politics.
Shortly before her husband's re-election last year, Naina unveiled her secret recipe for a chocolate cake in a Russian television interview designed at boosting Yeltsin's image as a family man.
The two have two daughters and four grandchildren.
